title: EU AI Act Article 50(4): When Must Deepfakes Be Disclosed?
context: 2026-08-27 — Article 50 transparency obligations are live (since 2 August 2026); deepfake disclosure is a standing duty now, ahead of the 2 December 2026 marking-grace deadline under Article 50(2).
body: Article 50(4) of the EU AI Act requires that a deployer of an AI system that generates or manipulates content constituting a deepfake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The duty applies to image, audio, and video content that would falsely appear authentic or truthful to a person — for example, a synthetic video of a real person saying something they never said. The obligation sits on the deployer, not the model provider, and it applies from the moment the content is put into circulation. It is not deferred to a future deadline: the transparency chapter (Article 50) took effect on 2 August 2026, so disclosure is a live duty today. There are three narrow exceptions — where the artificial nature is obvious from the circumstances, where the content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, or fictional work (with appropriate labelling that does not hamper display or enjoyment), or where law-enforcement use is authorised — and each exception still requires the manipulated nature to be indicated in some form. In practice, a compliant deployer labels synthetic media with a visible or machine-readable marker, keeps an internal record of what was generated, and treats disclosure as the default rather than the exception. The Council of AI measurement posture applies directly here: disclosure is a monitored containment discipline, not provable isolation. You cannot guarantee that no synthetic content will ever escape a labelled pipeline, but you can prove — through a verified measurement credential — that the disclosure was applied and recorded at the point of release. That converts a self-attested 'we disclosed it' into an auditable 'here is the signed record of the disclosure'.
